prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B009 as a single part with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After reading the full exchange and the chair's questions I hold it for reasons of content, not because six members converged on it. The Kane-Mele paper defined a Z2 invariant for time-reversal-symmetric band structures and predicted protected helical edge states. Molenkamp's group then observed the corresponding edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells, where band inversion is controlled by well thickness. That is a prediction and an observation that match, and about two decades of transport, ARPES and STM work in many materials have confirmed the picture. On the chair's question about the 2016 prize: that prize recognised topological phase transitions and topological phases in model low-dimensional systems. B009 shows that the band structure of an ordinary non-magnetic insulator carries a topological invariant that forces conducting boundary states, and it shows this in real crystals. I would let the citation state that difference through its wording, namely a classification of band structures by a Z2 invariant, and a first realisation in a material. On 2D versus 3D, I restrict the citation to the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators as introduced by Kane and Mele, with the HgTe realisation as the experimental anchor. I do not claim the three-dimensional ARPES work as part of this prize. I would rather say openly that it is a separate step with its own claimants than stretch three names across it.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection stays serious and I do not think the three-name limit can remove it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang specified HgTe as the material, and Hasan's group provided the first three-dimensional observations. Neither is among the credited trio, and Hasan is on the shortlist as a fourth name. If the committee judges that the 3D observation is the larger part of the story, then B009 as drawn credits the smaller half of it. The incrementalism objection after 2016 is weaker than Kroll and Danielsson suggest but it is not zero. The direct technological payoff is still limited, and I rely on my own recollection of the chronology, since the supplied materials do not settle the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang timing.

responses.point: Kroll sees B026 as the cleanest case of a measurement discovery with a clear two-name credit, treats the 2005 and 2012 overlap as the main risk, and considers the incrementalism objection to B009 partly valid.
responses.response: I take B026 seriously, and the chair's question is fair: the credit boundary is cleaner than for B009. But your own case_against states the problem. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize supply the tools and the clock concept, and the supplied materials do not settle magic-wavelength priority, so I cannot judge it from the record. What I can judge is that B026 is a large step in accuracy within precision metrology, whereas B009 introduced a new classification. I want a prize to be a discovery or an invention, as I said in my lecture reported by Tohoku, and I find that stronger for B009. I would not oppose B026 and I have now moved it up to my first alternative. If your recusal discussion on Hall's laboratory leaves you less able to carry B026, I do not think that should be the reason it fails. I would still need the committee to be explicit about the separation from earlier timekeeping prizes.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the Katori concept and the Ye push to 1e-18 are two identifiable contributions, that overlap with earlier prizes is answerable, and that B009's breadth of support should not be mistaken for the committee's centre of gravity.
responses.response: I agree with your last point and I have tried to apply it to myself: six supporters is a count and does not settle the physics. On the physics, your two-contribution description of B026 is persuasive, and I accept that the overlap objection is answerable in principle. Where I differ is the reading of 'discovery'. The magic-wavelength idea and its realisation open a new regime of precision, but the underlying quantum system, a cold-atom optical transition read out by a comb, is the one earlier prizes already recognised. In B009 the object is new: a topological invariant for band structure with protected edge conduction, observed in a material. If the committee decided that B026 is the cleaner credit, I could vote for it as my second choice without reservation about the names.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps Mele for the third slot and expects the citation to be narrow, but acknowledges that the contest with Hasan is real and that the 3D step may be a different, larger prize.
responses.response: We are close, and I want to be precise about where I stop. I keep Mele because the Z2 invariant is the common conceptual root of the HgTe observation and of the later 3D work, and because dropping the second theorist would leave the prediction with one name. In round 2 I agree with you that the citation should name the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators and say nothing about the 3D observation. Where I would not follow you is any wording so narrow that it hides the real structure of the field. I would accept a short explanatory text for the public that acknowledges Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan by name as contributors to the same development, without attaching credit to the prize.

responses.point: Eriksson separates the 2D and 3D steps and notes that the credit boundary is uncomfortable but accepts the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio, while saying his own DFT work makes the band-inversion story convincing.
responses.response: Your point about band inversion and spin-orbit coupling is the one that most sharpens my own view. The HgTe result is more than an observation of a predicted edge channel, since band inversion at a critical well thickness gives a controllable switch between trivial and topological regimes, and the BHZ model describes exactly that. This works in favour of the experimental credit to Molenkamp. It also makes the BHZ omission harder to wave away, and I accept your view that the committee should treat it as an acknowledged cost. I do not follow you in separating 2D and 3D as two prizes this year, but if the committee prefers that split, I agree it would leave the 3D step with its own natural candidates, which is the argument for citing the QSH state narrowly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Mele rather than Hasan in the third slot, and whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be handled in the public text without implying credit.
Whether the 2D and 3D steps should be treated as one discovery. I treat them as separate, and the answer decides whether B009 is complete.
Magic-wavelength priority and the competing claims of other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups for B026, which I cannot verify from the supplied materials.
The separation from the 2016 prize rests on my reading of the chronology and of what that prize covered, and some members see B009 as a continuation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B009 or for the alternatives I name, B026 and B033. My connections (Chalmers colleagues, David Clarke at IBM, Japanese academic exchanges, the international microscopy federation) are not tied to any credited name on this shortlist. I note again that my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson works in the circuit QED field relevant to B010, which I do not propose. I have no tie to Kroll's Boulder connection and see no reason it should affect how I read B026.
